power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The authors thank all participants for their participation in the study.
We also acknowledge the Servicio de Resonancia Magnética para Investigaciones Biomédicas (SEGAI) at the University of La Laguna for providing the MRI facilities.
Inhibitory control is a fundamental component of executive functioning that enables individuals to suppress dominant or prepotent responses in favour of contextually appropriate alternatives.

Although inhibitory control is often studied as overt motor responses, it also operates on internally generated representations, suppressing memories, thoughts, and verbal associations (Diamond, 2013).
text.formatted: Although inhibitory control is often studied as overt motor responses, it also operates on internally generated representations, suppressing memories, thoughts, and verbal associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Diamond, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: One such process is semantic inhibition, which involves inhibiting highly activated verbal or conceptual representations to allow the selection of contextually appropriate alternatives (Burgess & Shallice, 1996; Cervera-Crespo & González-Alvarez, 2017).
text.formatted: One such process is semantic inhibition, which involves inhibiting highly activated verbal or conceptual representations to allow the selection of contextually appropriate alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Burgess & Shallice, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cervera-Crespo & González-Alvarez, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Impairments in semantic inhibition have been reported across neuropsychiatric conditions characterized by impaired cognitive control (Wang et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Impairments in semantic inhibition have been reported across neuropsychiatric conditions characterized by impaired cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Wang et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, understanding the neural mechanisms supporting semantic inhibition may provide valuable insights into forms of inhibitory dysfunction that extend beyond the motor domain.

Inhibitory dysfunction has long been implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) where it may contribute to the characteristic persistence of intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviours (Norman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Inhibitory dysfunction has long been implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) where it may contribute to the characteristic persistence of intrusive thoughts and repetitive behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Norman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Most evidence, however, comes from motor paradigms, such as the Stop-Signal and Go-NoGo tasks, which predominantly capture impairments in response inhibition, that have been closely linked to compulsive tendencies (Bannon et al., 2002; Norman et al., 2019).

text.text: Neuroimaging studies using these paradigms have consistently implicated dysfunction within cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits in OCD (Pauls et al., 2014; Tomiyama et al., 2022; van Velzen et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Neuroimaging studies using these paradigms have consistently implicated dysfunction within cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits in OCD <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Pauls et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Tomiyama et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">van Velzen et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Altered recruitment of the presupplementary motor area (preSMA) during inhibitory control has been reported in patients with OCD and, importantly, in their unaffected first-degree relatives (de Wit et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Altered recruitment of the presupplementary motor area (preSMA) during inhibitory control has been reported in patients with OCD and, importantly, in their unaffected first-degree relatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(de Wit et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These observations suggest that abnormal preSMA function may reflect a candidate neural marker of vulnerability to obsessive-compulsive symptomatology rather than a consequence of the clinical disorder itself.
The predominance of motor paradigms leaves an important question unresolved.
Typically, the symptoms of OCD include not only repetitive actions but also persistent thoughts, images, doubts, and urges.

Studying the suppression of verbal and conceptual representations offers a means of testing whether inhibitory alterations associated with obsessive-compulsive tendencies extend beyond the motor domain.
Consequently, the Hayling Sentence Completion Task (HSCT) is particularly relevant for assessing semantic inhibition in OCD.
The task contrasts completion of a sentence with its expected ending with suppression of that dominant completion in favour of an unrelated response.
Difficulty in suppressing a strongly activated sentence completion word may be related to the difficulty to disengage from habitual or intrusive cognitive content.

Behavioural studies have reported altered Hayling-task performance in OCD (Doolub et al., 2023; Van der Linden et al., 2005), and electrophysiological evidence has also linked semantic inhibition to obsessive-compulsive tendencies (Iyoki & Kawasaki, 2019).

text.text: However, the neural substrates of semantic inhibition in relation to OCD symptomatology remain poorly characterized.
OCD is not an all-or-none diagnostic category.
Instead, obsessions and compulsive tendencies vary along a continuum in the general population (Abramovitch et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Instead, obsessions and compulsive tendencies vary along a continuum in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abramovitch et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, several of its core features, such as compulsive behaviors and rumination, are increasingly conceptualized as transdiagnostic processes that cut across multiple psychiatric disorders (Fullana et al., 2010; Gillan et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Moreover, several of its core features, such as compulsive behaviors and rumination, are increasingly conceptualized as transdiagnostic processes that cut across multiple psychiatric disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Fullana et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Gillan et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, complementary to the study of diagnosed OCD, a dimensional approach can be an effective research strategy by examining whether individuals differing in obsessive-compulsive traits also vary inhibitory processing.
Studying participants with lower and elevated trait levels also reduces confounding by medication, illness duration, and previous treatment.
This approach is particularly informative when the aim is to identify candidate mechanisms of vulnerability rather than consequences of established disorder.
Within the supplementary motor complex, the preSMA and SMA proper are anatomically adjacent but differ in their connectivity and functional organization.

The preSMA occupies a more rostral position and has been particularly implicated in higher-order aspects of action control, including response selection and the inhibition of prepotent responses, whereas SMA proper is more closely associated with motor-related processes (Nachev et al., 2008).

text.text: This functional distinction is paralleled by differences in connectivity, with the preSMA showing prominent connections with prefrontal and anterior cingulate regions, whereas SMA proper is more strongly associated with posterior parietal and motor circuitry (Lioumis et al., 2025).

text.text: These differences make the distinction between preSMA and SMA proper particularly relevant when examining forms of inhibitory control that extend beyond the motor domain.
The present study used an fMRI adaptation of the HSCT to investigate the neural correlates of semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive-compulsive traits.
Complementary whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest analyses in the preSMA and adjacent SMA proper were performed.
We expected inhibition trials to produce greater behavioral cost and stronger preSMA recruitment than initiation trials.
We further examined whether inhibition-related modulation in the preSMA and SMA proper differed between lower and elevated obsessive-compulsive traits.
In this way, the study tested whether neural alterations associated with obsessive-compulsive tendencies extend from motor inhibition to the control of prepotent semantic representations.
Recruitment for the fMRI experiment started with an online screening protocol implemented via Google Forms, which was responded to by 963 participants.
All of them were native Spanish speakers, undergraduate students from the University of La Laguna (Spain).

The initial screening battery included the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) (Sanz Fernández et al., 2003), the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAM-A) (Lobo et al., 2002), and the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) (Vega-Dienstmaier et al., 2002) to assess depressive symptoms, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive traits, respectively.

text.text: The BDI-II and HAM-A were used to exclude participants with elevated depressive or anxiety symptoms, respectively.
Participants were selected on the basis of Y-BOCS scores to obtain groups differing markedly in obsessive-compulsive symptom severity.
Individuals scoring between 8 and 10 (mild range) were selected for the control group, whereas those scoring between 22 and 28 were considered for the high-OCD-trait group.
This selection was intended to provide groups with contrasting levels of obsessive-compulsive traits rather than to establish clinical diagnostic categories.
Participants were excluded if they reported any psychiatric diagnosis within the past two years or current use of psychotropic medication.

Additional exclusion criteria included contraindications for MRI scanning, such as the presence of orthodontic appliances, metallic implants that could not be safely removed, or severe claustrophobia.
Only participants who were both native Spanish speakers and right-handed were included.
The final sample comprised 40 participants, with 20 individuals in the high-OCD-trait group and 20 in the control group.
The control group comprised 10 men and 10 women, whereas the high-OCD-trait group comprised 6 men and 14 women.
The mean age in the high-OCDtrait group was M = 21.45 years (SD = 6.14), and in the control group M = 22.65 years (SD = 4.76).
No significant differences were found between groups in age (Welch's t(35.77) = 0.69, p = .494) or sex distribution (Fisher's exact test, p = .333).

The Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) is widely regarded as the gold standard for assessing the presence and severity of obsessive-compulsive symptoms in clinical and research contexts (Goodman, Price, Rasmussen, Mazure, Delgado, et al., 1989; Goodman, Price, Rasmussen, Mazure, Fleischmann, et al., 1989).

text.text: The scale consists of 10 items, grouped into two subscales (obsessions and compulsions) each comprising five items that evaluate time spent, interference, distress, resistance, and control over symptoms.

Responses are rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (no symptoms) to 4 (extreme symptoms), yielding a total score from 0 to 40, where higher scores indicate greater severity of OCD symptomatology.

Interpretation of Y-BOCS scores typically follows established cutoffs: scores of 0-7 indicate subclinical symptoms, 8-15 mild symptoms, 16-23 moderate symptoms, 24-31 severe symptoms, and 32-40 extreme symptoms.
A Spanish-language version of the Y-BOCS has demonstrated good reliability and validity for the assessment of obsessive-compulsive symptom severity (Vega-Dienstmaier et al., 2002).

text.text: A modified version of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task was implemented to assess semantic inhibitory control during magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
The task comprised 80 unique incomplete sentences presented auditorily.
Each sentence was presented twice, once in each of the two response conditions, yielding 160 total trials.
A colored frame indicated whether participants should select a contextually appropriate completion (green; initiation) or inhibit that response and select an unrelated word (red; inhibition).
Three candidate completions were presented visually.
The complete set of sentence frames and response alternatives is provided in Supplementary Table S1.

text.text: The 80 incomplete sentences were selected from a standardized set of 142 Spanish HSCT sentences (Jan et al., 2024).

text.text: To determine the candidate completions, an independent normative study was performed with 30 participants, who did not take part in the fMRI experiment.
These participants were presented with each incomplete sentence and asked to provide the most appropriate completion.
Contexts for which the same completion was produced by over 96% of participants (e.g., words with a cloze probability of 1 or near to 1), were retained to serve as the "correct" response.

For each sentence frame, two additional options were created: an "unrelated" word with no semantic or phonological association with the correct completion, and a word semantically or phonologically "related" to it.
The related option was included to increase the difficulty of the choice in semantic inhibition trials.
All three options were grammatically compatible with the sentence context, and matched for word class, gender and number.

The options were selected to be comparable in word length, lexical frequency, familiarity and imageability according to norms from the Spanish EsPal database (Duchon et al., 2013), as shown in Table 1.

The fMRI experiment employed an event-related design comprising 80 Initiation and 80 Inhibition trials.
The 160 trials were presented in two independently randomized sets of 80 trials, each containing 40 trials per condition.
The positions of the correct, related, and unrelated response options were randomized across trials.
Each trial began with a fixation cross presented for 1 s, followed by the auditory presentation of an incomplete sentence.
Each auditory file lasted 3.5 s and contained a variable period of leading silence so that the spoken sentences ended at approximately the same time across items.
Following the auditory sentence offset, a blank screen was displayed for a jittered interval of 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 s prior to the response cue.
The cue -a red or green frame indicating the response condition-was presented first, followed 500 ms later by the three response options.
These options remained visible until the participant responded or until the end of the trial.
Participants selected an option using an MRI-compatible three-button response pad operated with the index, middle, or ring finger.
They were instructed to respond as quickly and accurately as possible and not to attempt to correct errors.
After a response, the screen remained blank for the remainder of the trial.
Trial onsets were spaced 10 s apart, yielding a total task duration of 26 min 40 s (see Figure 1).

text.text: Participants listened to each incomplete sentence via MRIcompatible headphones, and the three completion options were displayed using the VisuaStim Digital System.

Prior to scanning, all participants completed a training session in a mock MRI environment to ensure full comprehension of the task requirements and to minimize anxiety or discomfort during the actual experiment.

Functional images were acquired on a 3 T GE SIGNA Premier MR scanner (GE Healthcare) using a 48-channel head coil and a gradient-echo echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence (TR = 2000 ms, TE = 21.6 ms, flip angle = 90°, matrix size = 64 × 64, 37 slices, 4 × 4 mm² in-plane resolution, slice thickness = 4 mm, no interslice gap).
Slices were acquired in an axial orientation aligned with the anterior commissure-posterior commissure (AC-PC) line and provided whole-brain coverage.

High-resolution anatomical images were acquired using a 3D T1-weighted MP-RAGE sequence (TR = 2413.3 ms, TE = 1.972 ms, TI = 1000 ms, flip angle = 8°, matrix size = 256 × 256, slice thickness = 1 mm).

Image preprocessing: Functional MRI data were preprocessed using Statistical Parametric Mapping software (SPM12; Wellcome Centre for Human Neuroimaging, London, UK) implemented in MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA).
Functional images were first corrected for head motion using rigid-body realignment with unwarping to reduce susceptibility-by-movement interactions.

Slice-timing correction was then applied using an interleaved ascending acquisition order (odd slices first), with slice 19 as the reference slice, followed by coregistration of the anatomical T1-weighted image to the mean functional image.
The deformation field obtained from segmentation of the coregistered T1-weighted image was then used to normalize the functional images to MNI space, resampled to 2 × 2 × 2 mm³ isotropic voxels.
Finally, the normalized functional images were spatially smoothed using a 10 × 10 × 10 mm³ FWHM Gaussian kernel.
Normalization quality was visually inspected for all participants before statistical analysis.
First-level statistical analysis: Individual subject analyses were performed within the framework of the General Linear Model (GLM).
Four regressors of interest were defined by crossing Task (Initiation vs.
Inhibition) and Sentence type (Sensory vs.
Action).
Each trial was modelled as an event (duration = 0 s) and convolved with the canonical hemodynamic response function (HRF).
Six head-motion parameters obtained during realignment were included as nuisance regressors.
Low-frequency signal drifts were removed using a high-pass filter with a cutoff period of 128 s, and temporal autocorrelations were modelled using a firstorder autoregressive [AR(1)] model.

Because the primary aim of the present study was to investigate semantic inhibition, the main task contrast collapsed across sentence type and compared Inhibition with Initiation (Inhibition > Initiation).

text.text: The present study examined the neural correlates of semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive-compulsive traits using the Hayling Sentence Completion Task during fMRI.
Although behavioural performance was comparable between groups, neuroimaging analyses revealed differences in task-related modulation of activity in the left presupplementary motor area (preSMA).
In the whole-brain analysis across participants the inhibition > initiation contrast identified the strongest peak of activation in this region.
text.formatted: In the whole-brain analysis across participants the inhibition > initiation contrast identified the strongest peak of activation in this region.

text.text: In the same analysis a differential peak modulation between high-OCD-trait and control participants was also observed in a cluster in the posterior preSMA region.

To explore this group effect in more detail, anatomically defined regions of interest (ROIs) were submitted to new analyses showing a significant Group × Condition interaction after familywise error correction (FWE) for multiple comparisons in the preSMA, although the interaction in the adjacent SMA proper did not survive FWE correction.

Together, these findings suggest that elevated obsessivecompulsive traits are associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition, even in the absence of measurable behavioural differences.

The involvement of the preSMA is consistent with prior evidence that this region plays a role in higher-order inhibitory control, including action control, response selection and the suppression of prepotent responses, whereas the adjacent SMA proper is more closely associated with motor-related processes (Nachev et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The involvement of the preSMA is consistent with prior evidence that this region plays a role in higher-order inhibitory control, including action control, response selection and the suppression of prepotent responses, whereas the adjacent SMA proper is more closely associated with motor-related processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Nachev et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings extend this framework to a task requiring participants to override strongly activated semantic representations.
Importantly, the Group × Condition interaction remained significant after FWE correction in the anatomically defined preSMA ROI, whereas the corresponding effect in the adjacent SMA proper did not.
This pattern is consistent with the established functional differentiation within the supplementary motor complex and supports a role for the preSMA in semantic inhibitory processing.

At first glance, the reduced inhibition-related modulation of the preSMA in participants with elevated obsessive-compulsive traits observed in this study contrasts with the increased activation during motor response inhibition reported in patients with OCD and their unaffected first-degree relatives (de Wit et al., 2012).
text.formatted: At first glance, the reduced inhibition-related modulation of the preSMA in participants with elevated obsessive-compulsive traits observed in this study contrasts with the increased activation during motor response inhibition reported in patients with OCD and their unaffected first-degree relatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(de Wit et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation may lie in the task demands.
Previous neuroimaging studies of OCD have frequently employed Stop-Signal and Go/No-Go tasks, which require participants to suppress prepotent or ongoing motor responses.
In contrast, the present task is primarily a cognitive inhibition task, requiring the suppression of a contextually dominant semantic response while maintaining the requirement to press a button.

In principle, the preSMA activation in the inhibition > initiation contrast could be associated not only with semantic suppression, but also with differences in response selection, conflict and task difficulty.
text.formatted: In principle, the preSMA activation in the inhibition > initiation contrast could be associated not only with semantic suppression, but also with differences in response selection, conflict and task difficulty.

text.text: However, because both initiation and inhibition trials involved the same response device and response mappings, the contrast reduces the role of differences in motor demands.
Thus, the apparently divergent patterns of preSMA recruitment may reflect differences in the inhibitory processes engaged by these paradigms.
These differences across inhibitory paradigms may also reflect the functional organization of the preSMA-SMA complex.

Whereas preSMA territories show prominent connections with prefrontal regions, SMA territories have more prominent connections with motor and posterior parietal circuitry (Nachev et al., 2008; Lioumis et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Whereas preSMA territories show prominent connections with prefrontal regions, SMA territories have more prominent connections with motor and posterior parietal circuitry <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Nachev et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Lioumis et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such anatomical organization provides a plausible framework for understanding how different forms of inhibitory control may differentially recruit medial frontal territories.

From this perspective, differences across OCD studies may reflect, at least in part, the specific inhibitory processes recruited by different paradigms rather than contradictory patterns of preSMA dysfunction.
However, the present study did not directly compare semantic and motor inhibition or assess connectivity within these circuits.
The proposed relationship between task demands and pre-SMA recruitment therefore remains a hypothesis for future investigation.
Beyond the preSMA, the exploratory whole-brain interaction also identified a cluster in the anterior cingulate cortex.

This finding is relevant to a recent meta-analysis (Uhre et al., 2022), which identified convergent abnormalities in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex when analyses were restricted to cognitive inhibition tasks, but found no convergent regional abnormalities across different inhibitory paradigms considered together.
text.formatted: This finding is relevant to a recent meta-analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Uhre et al., 2022)</ref>, which identified convergent abnormalities in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex when analyses were restricted to cognitive inhibition tasks, but found no convergent regional abnormalities across different inhibitory paradigms considered together.

text.text: Although the cognitive inhibition tasks in the meta-analysis differ from semantic inhibition, these findings suggest that the neural differences associated with obsessive-compulsive symptomatology may depend on the specific inhibitory processes examined.
The present anterior cingulate finding, however, did not survive whole-brain correction and should be treated as preliminary.
Additional clusters were observed in the midbrain and cerebellum.
According to the AAL3 atlas, the midbrain cluster partially overlapped the dorsal raphe region.

This observation is noteworthy given evidence of serotonergic alterations in OCD, including reduced serotonin transporter availability in the midbrain and brainstem and altered functional connectivity of the raphe nucleus (Kim et al., 2019; Pastre et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This observation is noteworthy given evidence of serotonergic alterations in OCD, including reduced serotonin transporter availability in the midbrain and brainstem and altered functional connectivity of the raphe nucleus <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kim et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Pastre et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, atlas overlap and the limited anatomical resolution of conventional fMRI are insufficient to identify the involvement of small brainstem nuclei reliably, and BOLD activity does not provide a direct measure of serotonergic function.

Several cerebellar clusters were also observed (e.g., lobule VI and Crus I), consistent with previous evidence of altered cerebellar recruitment during inhibitory control in OCD (Norman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Several cerebellar clusters were also observed (e.g., lobule VI and Crus I), consistent with previous evidence of altered cerebellar recruitment during inhibitory control in OCD <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Norman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The absence of behavioural differences requires careful consideration.
Both groups showed the expected increase in reaction times and error rate during semantic inhibition, but neither measure showed a significant Group × Condition interaction.
Thus, the neural differences in preSMA recruitment were not accompanied by a corresponding difference in behavioural performance.

Similar dissociations between behavioural performance and neural measures have been reported in previous neuroimaging studies of inhibitory control in OCD (Hampshire et al., 2020; Lillevik Thorsen et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Similar dissociations between behavioural performance and neural measures have been reported in previous neuroimaging studies of inhibitory control in OCD <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hampshire et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lillevik Thorsen et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, this dissociation suggests that similar observed performance can accompany different patterns of pre-SMA recruitment.
It does not, however, establish behavioural equivalence or determine whether the neural difference reflects compensation, altered processing efficiency or a different task strategy.
Several limitations qualify the conclusions in this study.

As the sample was selected on the basis of elevated obsessive-compulsive traits obtained in self-report questionnaires rather than clinical OCD diagnosis, the findings cannot be directly generalized to patients with OCD.
However, studying individuals not taking psychiatric medication reduces a potential source of confounding commonly encountered in clinical OCD research.
The sample size may also have limited sensitivity to behavioural differences and smaller neural effects.
Additionally, the groups were not fully balanced by sex.
Although the ROIs were anatomically defined, their choice after an exploratory whole-brain analysis warrants caution in treating the ROI result as independent confirmation.

Replication in a larger sample, with prospectively specified ROI analyses and direct comparisons of semantic and motor inhibition within the same participants, would help establish the robustness of the effects, and whether differences in preSMA recruitment depend on the specific form of inhibitory control being examined.

The present study showed altered task-related modulation of the left preSMA during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive-compulsive traits, whereas the corresponding Group × Condition interaction in the adjacent SMA proper did not reach statistical significance.
Despite comparable behavioural performance between groups, these findings highlight the relevance of the preSMA to semantic inhibitory processing associated with obsessivecompulsive traits.
More broadly, they support the view that inhibitory control should not be considered a unitary process when investigating obsessive-compulsive symptomatology.
Different inhibitory paradigms may therefore provide complementary information about inhibitory control in relation to obsessive-compulsive symptomatology.
